  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();

<br class="ltx_break">Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models</h1>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Modern compilers optimize programs through a sequence of modular passes over intermediate representations (IR). While this pass-by-pass paradigm offers engineering benefits, it suffers from a pass coordination problem: locally beneficial transformations may block more profitable optimizations in later stages. This limitation stems from the lack of an explicit notion of optimization intent, defined as a holistic strategy for coordinating multiple transformations toward a global performance objective.
Recent LLM–based approaches formulate IR optimization as an end-to-end generation task, thereby avoiding the traditional pass-by-pass structure. However, optimization intent remains implicit in these methods, forcing models to jointly infer optimization strategy and generate low-level transformations, which limits both correctness and performance.
We propose IntOpt, the first intent-driven IR optimizer that explicitly separates high-level optimization intent from low-level analysis and transformation. IntOpt organizes IR optimization into three stages: intent formulation, intent refinement, and intent realization, enabling globally coordinated transformations.
Experiments show that IntOpt achieves 90.5% verified correctness and 2.660× average speedup on 200-program test set, outperforming state-of-the-art LLM-based optimizers in both correctness and performance, and surpassing modern compiler with the <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> option on 37 benchmarks with speedups of up to 272.60×.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Modern compilers leverage intermediate representations (IR) to enable compilation that is independent of both programming languages and hardware architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aho et al., 2006</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lattner and Adve, 2004</a>)</cite>. By optimizing at the IR level, which abstracts away language- and hardware-specific details, compilers can improve the program execution efficiency (referred to as “<span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">performance</span>”) across diverse programming languages, target architectures, and application domains, ranging from traditional scientific computing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moses et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bezanson et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Özen et al., 2018</a>)</cite> to modern AI workloads with specialized tensor operations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lattner et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sabne, 2020</a>)</cite>. Consequently, designing effective IR optimization strategies has remained significant in compiler construction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, the effectiveness of IR-level optimization is fundamentally constrained by <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how modern compilers organize optimization</em>. In practice, modern compilers decompose IR optimization into a sequence of passes, each implemented as a modular unit that targets a specific optimization, such as loop unrolling or constant propagation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lattner and Adve, 2004</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stanier and Watson, 2013</a>)</cite>. These passes make decisions by analyzing optimization-related information derived from the IR (hereafter referred to as <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">“analysis”</span>) to assess whether a transformation will be beneficial. Although this <span id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">pass-by-pass paradigm</span> offers clear engineering benefits in terms of modularity and maintainability, it inherently suffers from a pass coordination problem: optimizations that are locally beneficial in early passes can inadvertently restrict or even prevent more profitable optimizations in later stages.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As illustrated in <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 1</span></a>(b), when the compiler optimizes the IR corresponding to the source code in <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 1</span></a>(a), the <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LICMPass</span> (loop-invariant code motion) hoists <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">D[i]</span> from <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{3}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{2}^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{2}^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> to eliminate redundant accesses in the inner loop. While this transformation is locally beneficial, it prevents the <span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LoopInterchangePass</span> from swapping the <span id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">i</span> and <span id="S1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">j</span> loops to improve memory locality. More critically, because <span id="S1.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LoopInterchangePass</span> cannot be applied, the subsequent <span id="S1.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LoopVectorizePass</span> also fails to vectorize <math id="S1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{4}^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>L</mi><mn>4</mn><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{4}^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>. As a result, the innermost loop retains a column-major access pattern for <span id="S1.p3.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">A[j][i]</span> and <span id="S1.p3.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">B[j][i]</span>, which inhibits effective SIMD utilization and ultimately leads to degraded performance.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18511v1/fig-cmp.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/166;" width="405" height="166" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison between existing IR optimization approaches and our <span id="S1.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span>. </span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This behavior arises from the lack of an explicit notion of <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">optimization intent</span>, which we define as a holistic strategy for coordinating multiple transformations toward a global performance objective. In compilers such as GCC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">GCC, 2026</a>)</cite> and LLVM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">LLVM, 2026c</a>)</cite>, this intent is implicit and fragmented across individual optimization passes. As shown in <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 1</span></a>(b), <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LICMPass</span> reduces memory operations, <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LoopInterchangePass</span> improves memory locality, and <span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LoopVectorizePass</span> targets SIMD optimization. However, without explicit global coordination, individual passes cannot anticipate how their transformations may enable or inhibit downstream optimization opportunities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kulkarni et al., 2006</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pallister et al., 2015</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Daya et al., 2025</a>)</cite> offer a promising way to address this limitation due to their strong program understanding and semantic reasoning capabilities. Prior LLM-based IR optimization methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cummins et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> formulate IR optimization as an end-to-end generation task that directly maps unoptimized IR to optimized IR, as shown in <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 1</span></a>(c), avoiding the traditional pass-by-pass structure in compilers. However, this reformulation does not fundamentally resolve the core issue: optimization intent remains implicit, now hidden within a black-box LLM generation process rather than fragmented across individual passes in compilers. Consequently, LLMs are forced to simultaneously infer optimization intent and generate precise transformations, which makes it challenging to guarantee both semantic correctness and consistent performance improvement. Our experiments in <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Improvement over LLM-based IR Optimizers ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec. 4.2</span></a> empirically reveal substantial room for improvement.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we propose <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span>, an <span id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">Int</span>ent-driven IR <span id="S1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">Opt</span>imizer that reformulates the modern compiler optimization paradigm by decoupling high-level optimization intent from low-level analysis and transformation, thereby enabling globally coordinated transformations. <span id="S1.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> achieves this goal by deconstructing the IR optimization process into three stages: <span id="S1.p6.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">intent formulation</span>, <span id="S1.p6.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">intent refinement</span>, and <span id="S1.p6.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">intent realization</span>. This pipeline mirrors how expert compiler engineers operate: first reasoning about optimization intent at a global level, then grounding it using program analysis to assess feasibility, and finally realizing it through concrete transformations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Muchnick, 1998</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Our key insight is that, although existing compilers encode optimization intent implicitly within hand-crafted passes, these intents capture valuable domain knowledge that LLMs can learn and make explicit. Building on this, <span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> first uses an LLM specialized in compiler optimization to infer an initial optimization strategy for a given program, representing a structured form of optimization intent. This strategy is then grounded and refined using compiler analysis. For example, in <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 1</span></a>(d), an initial strategy of vectorization with <span id="S1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;2 x double&gt;</span> is refined to <span id="S1.p7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;4 x double&gt;</span> based on hardware-aware analysis. The refined strategy subsequently guides optimized IR generation, ensuring that transformations are globally coordinated. During the intent refinement and realization stage, <span id="S1.p7.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> leverages GPT-5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025</a>)</cite> and its pre-training knowledge to explore optimization opportunities beyond those captured by existing compiler passes, as shown in <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Case Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec. 4.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate <span id="S1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> on 200 LLVM IR programs and achieve significant improvements over both end-to-end LLM-based optimizers and traditional compiler. Our results highlight the importance of making optimization intent explicit for globally coordinated and semantically grounded IR optimization. We hope our findings will facilitate more research on intent-driven compiler optimization in this field.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18511v1/fig-overview.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/155;" width="452" height="155" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S1.F2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of <span id="S1.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">To sum up, our main contribution includes:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:2ex;">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Intent-driven IR optimization framework.</span> We propose the first intent-driven IR optimization framework that decouples optimization intent from concrete IR transformation, enabling more effective and reliable optimizations.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compiler-knowledge-grounded IR optimization.</span> We develop a novel approach that integrates structured compiler knowledge to guide LLMs in IR optimization.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comprehensive evaluation.</span> <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> achieves 90.5% verified correctness and 2.660<math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> average speedup on 200-program test set, outperforming state-of-the-art LLM-based optimizers by 7.0%-31.5% in correctness and up to 1.603<math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> in performance, while also surpassing LLVM <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> on 37 benchmark programs with speedups up to 272.60<math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Works</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Traditional IR Optimization in Compilers.</span>
Modern compilers such as LLVM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">LLVM, 2026c</a>)</cite> and GCC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">GCC, 2026</a>)</cite> perform IR optimization through a fixed sequence of passes (e.g., <span id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span>), where each pass applies a specific transformation guided by a predefined set of compiler analysis and hand-crafted heuristics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lattner and Adve, 2004</a>)</cite>. To provide flexibility, compilers expose numerous configuration options that allow users to enable or disable specific optimizations or adjust heuristic parameters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Muchnick, 1998</a>)</cite>. However, interactions among optimization passes are often complex and difficult to predict <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kulkarni et al., 2006</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pallister et al., 2015</a>)</cite>, making it challenging to reason about or control global optimization strategies for a given program.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Autotuning for Compiler Optimization.</span>
Building on the pass-by-pass optimization infrastructure, a line of work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ansel et al., 2014</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al., 2025</a>)</cite> has explored autotuning approaches that search over compiler options, optimization flags, or pass configurations to improve performance. While these methods can yield performance gains, it suffers from several inherent limitations. First, the search process is time-consuming, as it requires repeated compilation (and, for runtime performance–oriented objectives, execution) under many configurations. Second, optimization options are coarse-grained: disabling, enabling, or reordering a pass affects all occurrences of that transformation across the entire program. For example, if loop-invariant code motion is disabled at the option level to avoid harming a particular loop (as in <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 1</span></a>(a)), other loops where LICM would be beneficial are also affected.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLMs for Compiler and Code Optimization.</span>
Recent work has begun to explore using LLMs for compiler construction and program optimization. Some approaches focus on enhancing compiler backend development efficiency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhong et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhong et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhong et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, while others target source-level program rewriting for vectorization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Taneja et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. More closely related to our work are efforts that apply LLMs directly to IR-level optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cummins et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, formulating optimization as an end-to-end generation task. While these methods bypass the traditional pass-by-pass pipeline, they typically rely on black-box generation without explicit representations of optimization intent.
In contrast, our work models optimization intent as an explicit intermediate step and integrates LLM-based reasoning with compiler knowledge to enable globally coordinated IR optimization.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Proposed Method: <span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span></h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To explicitly model and reason about optimization intent during compiler optimization, we propose <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span>, an intent-driven IR optimization framework. As illustrated in <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 2</span></a>, <span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> contains three stages: intent formulation (<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Intent Formulation ‣ 3 Proposed Method: IntOpt ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec. 3.1</span></a>), intent refinement (<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Intent Refinement ‣ 3 Proposed Method: IntOpt ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec. 3.2</span></a>), and intent realization (<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Intent Realization ‣ 3 Proposed Method: IntOpt ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec. 3.3</span></a>). This structure decouples high-level optimization intent from low-level analysis and transformations, allowing <span id="S3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> to make globally coordinated IR optimization.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Intent Formulation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The intent formulation stage generates an initial optimization strategy <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, which serves as a structured instantiation of the optimization intent, for a given input IR program <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S=\mathcal{F}_{\theta}(P)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S=\mathcal{F}_{\theta}(P)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes an optimization-specialized LLM parameterized by <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, fine-tuned on compiler optimization behaviors. The strategy <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> is represented as an ordered sequence of transformation actions <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\langle a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n}\rangle" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\langle a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n}\rangle</annotation></semantics></math>, where each action <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> specifies in natural language which transformation to apply to which program region (e.g., “Vectorize line <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{3}</annotation></semantics></math> with <span id="S3.SS1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;2 x double&gt;</span>”).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Representing actions in natural language avoids prematurely constraining the optimization action space, allowing the model to reason over a richer and more flexible space of optimization strategies. Despite this flexibility, the problem remains tractable: while the space of semantically equivalent IR programs is vast, the set of transformation actions exposed by a modern compiler is finite and curated by compiler developers. This bounded action set makes intent formulation amenable to data-driven learning from a modestly sized dataset. Consequently, to fine-tune the intent formulation model <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, we construct a dataset by distilling optimization intents from compiler behaviors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dataset Construction.</span>
As shown in <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 2</span></a>(a), we first collect a diverse set of IR programs from IR-OptSet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>,
an IR-oriented dataset designed to trigger representative optimization transformations encountered in real compiler optimization scenarios.
We compile the collected programs using LLVM 19.1.0 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">LLVM, 2026c</a>)</cite> with the <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> flag to obtain paired unoptimized and optimized IR programs <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(P^{\text{unopt}},P^{\text{opt}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mtext>unopt</mtext></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mtext>opt</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(P^{\text{unopt}},P^{\text{opt}})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> enables a broad range of optimization passes.
We then distill optimization intent from the observed end-to-end optimization behavior <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P^{\text{unopt}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>P</mi><mtext>unopt</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P^{\text{unopt}}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P^{\text{opt}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>P</mi><mtext>opt</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P^{\text{opt}}</annotation></semantics></math> by using GPT-5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025</a>)</cite> to infer the underlying optimization strategy <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> for each IR pair. The resulting triples – unoptimized IR <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P^{\text{unopt}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>P</mi><mtext>unopt</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P^{\text{unopt}}</annotation></semantics></math>, optimized IR <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P^{\text{opt}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>P</mi><mtext>opt</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P^{\text{opt}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and inferred strategy <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> – constitute the training dataset <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model Training.</span>
We fine-tune LLM Compiler FTD 13B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cummins et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, an LLM for IR optimization, on <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> to obtain the optimization-specialized LLM <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>. The training objective is to minimize the negative log-likelihood of generating the ground-truth optimization strategy <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> conditioned on the unoptimized IR program <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P^{\text{unopt}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>P</mi><mtext>unopt</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P^{\text{unopt}}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(P^{\text{unopt}},S)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}\left[\log p_{\theta}(S\mid P^{\text{unopt}})\right]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mtext>unopt</mtext></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mtext>unopt</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(P^{\text{unopt}},S)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}\left[\log p_{\theta}(S\mid P^{\text{unopt}})\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">The choice of a 13B-parameter model is deliberate: intent formulation is primarily pattern recognition over program structures and compiler optimization behaviors, which does not require the extensive reasoning capabilities needed for subsequent refinement and realization stages. This design balances effectiveness with computational efficiency.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Intent Refinement</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The intent formulation stage produces an initial optimization strategy that specifies which transformations to apply and in what order.
Although this strategy captures high-level optimization intent learned from compiler behaviors, it is inferred in a data-driven manner and may miss key constraints from program semantics or target-specific requirements. The intent refinement stage therefore grounds the initial strategy in concrete compiler analysis and revises it when needed, ensuring that each proposed transformation is applicable and well-informed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A key challenge of intent refinement is identifying which compiler analysis is necessary to refine the given strategy <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>. Since different transformations rely on different types of analysis, retrieving all available analysis is both inefficient and unnecessary.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To address this challenge, we design an analysis-aware retrieval mechanism that explicitly captures the relationship between transform passes and their required analysis. By constructing a structured compiler knowledge base and using it to retrieve only the analysis relevant to each transformation action in <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, the refinement process concentrates on the most informative analysis signals while avoiding unnecessary overhead.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compiler Knowledge Base Construction.</span> We construct a structured knowledge base <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{K}</annotation></semantics></math> that catalogs compiler optimization passes (i.e., transform passes) and their analysis dependencies. Each entry <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\in\mathcal{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\in\mathcal{K}</annotation></semantics></math> is represented as:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=(ID,Desc,Deps)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=(ID,Desc,Deps),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ID" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ID</annotation></semantics></math> uniquely identifies a transform pass (corresponding to its pass class name, e.g., <span id="S3.SS2.p4.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">LoopVectorizePass</span>), <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Desc" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Desc</annotation></semantics></math> provides a natural-language description of the pass’s functionality and optimization objectives, and <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Deps" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Deps</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the set of compiler analysis required by the pass.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We build <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{K}</annotation></semantics></math> through an automatic extraction process from the LLVM compiler infrastructure. First, we parse <span id="S3.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">llvm/lib/Passes/PassRegistry.def</span>, which enumerates all transform passes, to obtain the set of pass identifiers <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ID" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ID</annotation></semantics></math>. For each pass, we then extract its functional description from the official LLVM pass documentation<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <a href="https://llvm.org/docs/Passes.html" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://llvm.org/docs/Passes.html</a></span></span></span> to populate the corresponding <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Desc" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Desc</annotation></semantics></math> field.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To extract the analysis dependencies <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Deps" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Deps</annotation></semantics></math>, we exploit a key design principle of LLVM: each transform pass must explicitly declare analysis passes it relies on by invoking <span id="S3.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">AnalysisManager::getResult</span> within its <span id="S3.SS2.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">run</span> method. Accordingly, LLVM provides a collection of analysis passes, each responsible for extracting specific optimization-related information from the IR programs to guide transformation decisions. This explicit dependency mechanism allows us to systematically trace which analysis passes are required by each transform pass, yielding a reliable and complete specification of its analysis requirements. For example, <span id="S3.SS2.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">LoopVectorizePass</span> requests loop-structure and target-specific analysis as follows:</p>
</div>

</div>
<div id="lstnumberx6" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">  </span><span id="lstnumberx6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">...</span>
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx7" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">}</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, we obtain the <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Deps" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Deps</annotation></semantics></math> field by locating each pass’s <span id="S3.SS2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">run</span> implementation under <span id="S3.SS2.p8.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">llvm/lib/ Transforms</span> and statically parsing all invocations of <span id="S3.SS2.p8.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">AnalysisManager::getResult</span>. As shown in <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 2</span></a>(b), the dependency set for <span id="S3.SS2.p8.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">LoopVectorizePass</span> is {<span id="S3.SS2.p8.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">LoopAnalysis</span>, <span id="S3.SS2.p8.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TargetLibraryAnalysis</span>}.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Retrieve Analysis Results.</span>
With the constructed compiler knowledge base <math id="S3.SS2.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{K}</annotation></semantics></math>, we retrieve the concrete compiler transform passes and their dependent analysis passes corresponding to each transformation action <math id="S3.SS2.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> in the initial optimization strategy <math id="S3.SS2.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>. Specifically, for each action <math id="S3.SS2.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, we treat the natural-language description of <math id="S3.SS2.p9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> as a query and match it against the document corpus <math id="S3.SS2.p9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{Desc(k)\}_{k\in\mathcal{K}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{Desc(k)\}_{k\in\mathcal{K}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Both the query and documents are represented using TF-IDF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2011</a>)</cite> with 1–3 gram tokenization, and the top-m matching passes are selected based on cosine similarity.</p>
<table id="S3.Ex4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex4X"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p9.2" class="ltx_p">Such design balances efficiency and coverage: top-m retrieval captures cases where multiple passes address similar goals (e.g., <span id="S3.SS2.p9.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">EarlyCSEPass</span>, <span id="S3.SS2.p9.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">DCEPass</span>, and <span id="S3.SS2.p9.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GVNPass</span> all perform redundancy elimination) while avoiding the computational overhead of indiscriminate analysis execution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Once the passes <math id="S3.SS2.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{k_{i}^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{k_{i}^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{m}</annotation></semantics></math> are identified, we retrieve their required analysis passes <math id="S3.SS2.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textit{Deps}(k_{i}^{(j)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">Deps</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textit{Deps}(k_{i}^{(j)})</annotation></semantics></math> from the knowledge base and invoke the LLVM compiler to generate the corresponding analysis results on the current IR program <math id="S3.SS2.p10.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{S}=\bigcup_{a_{i}\in S}\bigcup_{j=1}^{m}\text{LLVM\_Generate}(\textit{Deps}(k_{i}^{(j)}),P)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">⋃</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">⋃</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><mrow><mtext>LLVM_Generate</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">Deps</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{S}=\bigcup_{a_{i}\in S}\bigcup_{j=1}^{m}\text{LLVM\_Generate}(\textit{Deps}(k_{i}^{(j)}),P)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p10.2" class="ltx_p">The analysis results are obtained through LLVM’s analysis inspection interfaces (e.g., <span id="S3.SS2.p10.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">opt -p=print&lt;analysis&gt;</span>), which generate analysis information in textual form. This information corresponds to the same analysis results that transform passes query during the compiler optimization process to ensure correctness and performance. As a result, they provide reliable information for downstream intent refinement and intent realization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p11.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p11.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Refinement.</span> Given the initial optimization strategy <math id="S3.SS2.p11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> and the retrieved analysis results <math id="S3.SS2.p11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{S}</annotation></semantics></math>, the refinement stage produces a refined strategy <math id="S3.SS2.p11.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>S</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{S}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{S}=\mathcal{G}(P,S,R_{S})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>S</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{S}=\mathcal{G}(P,S,R_{S})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p11.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p11.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the LLM (GPT-5) that performs intent refinement by reasoning over the program, initial strategy, and compiler analysis information. The prompt template used during refinement is provided in <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Prompt Template for IntOpt ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p12.1" class="ltx_p">This refinement process validates and enhances the initial strategy in <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Intent Formulation ‣ 3 Proposed Method: IntOpt ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a> by grounding it in compiler analysis information: it filters infeasible transformations based on program constraints, while leveraging both analysis information and the LLM’s pretraining knowledge to refine the transformations in ways that may exceed conventional compiler heuristics. The resulting strategy <math id="S3.SS2.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>S</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{S}</annotation></semantics></math> is constraint-aware and analytically informed, providing a reliable bridge between intent formulation and concrete intent realization.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Intent Realization</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The intent realization stage finally applies the strategy <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>S</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{S}</annotation></semantics></math> on the unoptimized IR program <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> to generate the optimized IR program <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{P}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{P}=\mathcal{G}(P,\hat{S},R_{S})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>S</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{P}=\mathcal{G}(P,\hat{S},R_{S})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the same LM (GPT-5) used in refinement. This stage synthesizes the optimized program by applying the transformation actions specified in <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>S</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{S}</annotation></semantics></math> while respecting the constraints encoded in the analysis results <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{S}</annotation></semantics></math>. The prompt template is provided in <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Prompt Template for IntOpt ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Through this three-stage pipeline – formulation, refinement, and realization – <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> transforms high-level optimization intent into concrete, well-informed IR transformations. Leveraging GPT-5 for intent refinement and realization allow <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> to explore optimization strategies beyond those typically produced by traditional fixed-pass compilers.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
