<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.1 </span>Dataset</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct all datasets from IR-OptSet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, an IR-oriented dataset designed to trigger representative optimization transformations encountered in real compiler optimization scenarios, and each IR sample (unoptimized IR plus optimized IR) is capped at 5,000 tokens. We randomly sample 4,000 programs to form the training set <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{INT}_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">INT</mtext><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{INT}_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> and 500 programs to form the validation set <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{INT}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">INT</mtext><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">val</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{INT}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For evaluation, we construct a separate test set <math id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{INT}_{\text{test}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">INT</mtext><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">test</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{INT}_{\text{test}}</annotation></semantics></math> of 200 IR samples through a multi-stage filtering process. First, we retain programs for which Alive2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lopes et al., 2021</a>)</cite> can verify semantic equivalence between the unoptimized IR and LLVM <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span>. Second, we exclude programs unsuitable for differential testing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">McKeeman, 1998</a>)</cite>, such as those with custom external functions, externally defined global variables, or non-deterministic behavior. This ensures that when LLM-based optimizers produce transformations beyond Alive2’s verification capability, differential testing can be reliably used for correctness validation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.2 </span>Baselines</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We include two categories of baselines for comparison:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">End-to-end LLM-based IR optimizers.</span> We consider both general-purpose and specialized LLM-based optimizers that directly map unoptimized IR to optimized IR.
Specifically, we evaluate three representative general-purpose LLMs with strong capabilities on code-related tasks:
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">GPT-5</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025</a>)</cite>,
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Claude Haiku 4.5</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025</a>)</cite>, and
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">DeepSeek-V3.2</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
All models are prompted using the template shown in <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Prompt Template for LLM-based Optimizers ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix C</span></a>.
We also compare against LLM Compiler <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cummins et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, a state-of-the-art specialized end-to-end IR optimizer, evaluating both the 7B and 13B parameter variants (<span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">LLM Compiler FTD 7B</span> and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">LLM Compiler FTD 13B</span>). To ensure a fair comparison, both LLM Compiler variants are fine-tuned on <math id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{INT}_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>INT</mtext><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{INT}_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{INT}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>INT</mtext><mtext>val</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{INT}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math> following <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Experimental Details ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix E</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compiler baseline.</span> We include <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">LLVM 19.1.0</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">LLVM, 2026c</a>)</cite> with the <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">-O3</span> optimization level as a compiler-level reference. <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> aggressively optimizes for execution speed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">LLVM, 2026b</a>)</cite> and represents a highly tuned IR optimization strategy.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.3 </span>Implementation Details</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the intent formulation stage of <span id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span>, we obtain the optimization-specialized LLM <math id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> in <span id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span>, using the <math id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{INT}_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>INT</mtext><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{INT}_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{INT}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>INT</mtext><mtext>val</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{INT}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math>, following the procedure described in <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Intent Formulation ‣ 3 Proposed Method: IntOpt ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec. 3.1</span></a>.
During the analysis results retrieval stage, we select the top-3 matching optimization passes and collect their corresponding LLVM analysis results, which are used to support the intent refinement stage.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.4 </span>Evaluation Metrics</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Correctness Verification.</span>
We employ a two-stage verification process to validate the <span id="S4.SS1.SSS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Correctness</span> of optimized IR programs. We first apply Alive2 to perform strict formal semantic equivalence checking between the optimized and unoptimized IR. Since Alive2 may time out on verifying programs with complex control flow or memory behaviors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lopes et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, we additionally apply differential testing when formal verification is infeasible. Specifically, we use LibFuzzer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">LLVM, 2026a</a>)</cite> to generate diverse test inputs and verify that optimized and unoptimized programs produce identical outputs across different execution paths. Details are provided in <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Correctness Validation via Differential Testing ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix F</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Performance Evaluation.</span>
We measure performance using the same inputs generated by LibFuzzer during correctness verification, reflecting execution behaviors across diverse control flow paths. Each program is executed for 10,000 iterations to obtain stable timing measurements and mitigate measurement noise.
We report <span id="S4.SS1.SSS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Performance</span> as speedup ratio:
<math id="S4.SS1.SSS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Speedup}=\text{RunTime(unopt)}/\text{RunTime(opt)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Speedup</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>RunTime(unopt)</mtext><mo>/</mo><mtext>RunTime(opt)</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Speedup}=\text{RunTime(unopt)}/\text{RunTime(opt)}</annotation></semantics></math>.
When an LLM-based optimizer generates incorrect IR, we assign a speedup of 0. More details are in  <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Performance Validation ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix G</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18511v1/fig-cmp-perf.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/121;" width="429" height="121" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Per-program speedup comparison between <span id="S4.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> and representative end-to-end LLM-based IR optimizers. Speedup differences within <math id="S4.F3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math>2% are considered equal to account for runtime variability.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18511v1/fig-cmp-o3.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/84;" width="405" height="84" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Performance comparison between <span id="S4.F4.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> and LLVM <span id="S4.F4.8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span>.
Speedup is defined as <math id="S4.F4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{RunTime}(\text{LLVM {-O3}})/\text{RunTime}(\text{opt})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>RunTime</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>LLVM </mtext><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">-O3</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mtext>RunTime</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>opt</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{RunTime}(\text{LLVM {-O3}})/\text{RunTime}(\text{opt})</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S4.F4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.98,1.02]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.98</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.02</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.98,1.02]</annotation></semantics></math> treated as equal.
<span id="S4.F4.8.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> matches LLVM <span id="S4.F4.8.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> on 105 programs and outperforms it on 37 (max <math id="S4.F4.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="272.60\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>272.60</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">272.60\times</annotation></semantics></math>); among 58 underperforming cases, most are slight slowdowns (27 in <math id="S4.F4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.90,0.98]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.90</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.98</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.90,0.98]</annotation></semantics></math>), and 19 are incorrect.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Improvement over LLM-based IR Optimizers</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first compare <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> with end-to-end LLM-based IR optimizers on the 200-sample benchmark <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{INT}_{\text{test}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>INT</mtext><mtext>test</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{INT}_{\text{test}}</annotation></semantics></math>. As shown in  <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 1</span></a>, <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> achieves the strongest overall results across all baselines in both correctness and performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Correctness.</span> Under Alive2-only verification, GPT-5 achieves the highest correctness rate among baselines (73.0%), while <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> attains a comparable rate of 71.0%. However, this metric is inherently limited by Alive2’s verification capability: even complex optimizations produced by LLVM <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> cannot always be verified <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lopes et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. When differential testing is incorporated, <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> achieves a verified correctness rate of 90.5%, surpassing all other baselines by 7.0%-31.5%. These results highlight <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> ’s advantage in reducing semantic errors over end-to-end LLM-based IR optimization methods.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Performance.</span>
<span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> achieves an average speedup of 2.660<math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> over the unoptimized IR, significantly outperforming all end-to-end LLM-based baselines.The strongest baseline, GPT-5, attains an average speedup of only 1.057<math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, resulting in a 1.603<math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> performance gap.
Beyond average performance, <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> also consistently dominates across all speedup thresholds, indicating that its performance gains are broadly distributed across the benchmark.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To better understand these improvements, we further compare <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> against the two strongest baselines, GPT-5 and LLM Compiler FTD 13B, on a per-program basis, as shown in <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1.4 Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 3</span></a>.
Against GPT-5, <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> achieves higher speedups on 62 programs, while the advantage is more pronounced against LLM Compiler FTD 13B, where <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> outperforms it on 118 programs.
Notably, when compared to the unoptimized IR, <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> attains a maximum speedup of up to <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="287.72\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>287.72</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">287.72\times</annotation></semantics></math> on a single program.
These results suggest that <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> is more effective at discovering and realizing aggressive yet profitable optimization opportunities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">

<span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_middle" style="width:345.0pt;">
<span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Answer to RQ.1:</span> By decoupling optimization intent formulation from concrete transformation generation, <span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> reduces semantic errors and is more effective at discovering profitable optimization opportunities than existing end-to-end LLM-based IR optimization approaches.</span>
</span></span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Improvement over Traditional Compiler</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further compare <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span>’s performance against LLVM <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span>, a highly optimized and widely adopted compiler optimization level.
<a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.1.4 Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 4</span></a> shows the comparison results.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> achieves performance comparable to LLVM <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> on 105 programs and outperforms it on <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">37</span> programs.
Among these improved cases, the per-program speedup distribution reveals a spectrum of performance gains: 5 programs exhibit substantial improvements with speedups greater than <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5\times</annotation></semantics></math>, while 13 programs achieve clear improvements exceeding <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.1\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.1\times</annotation></semantics></math>.
Notably, the program that achieves the highest speedup in <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1.4 Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 3</span></a> also attains the highest performance improvement over LLVM <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span>, with a speedup of up to <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="272.60\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>272.60</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">272.60\times</annotation></semantics></math>.
We analyze this case in detail in <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Case Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec. 4.4</span></a>, illustrating how <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> can uncover optimization opportunities that go beyond the capabilities of the traditional compiler.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18511v1/fig-casestudy.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/243;" width="452" height="243" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Case study illustrating how <span id="S4.F5.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> explores optimization opportunities beyond the traditional pass-by-pass compiler paradigm.

<td id="S4.T2.8.1.4.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:2.7pt;padding-right:2.7pt;"><span id="S4.T2.8.1.4.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">15.0% (30)</span></td>

</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Case Analysis</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To provide deeper insights into the intent-driven optimization mechanism, we present two representative cases that illustrate how <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> explores optimization opportunities beyond the traditional pass-by-pass compiler paradigm.
Due to space constraints, we present pseudo-code representations of the IR; the full code listings are provided in <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Case Study ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix H</span></a>.
As shown in <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 Improvement over Traditional Compiler ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 5</span></a>, traditional compilers primarily optimize programs by matching pre-defined patterns in passes designed by compiler developers and applying transformations (e.g., eliminating stack-based load/store operations).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast, <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> performs intent-guided optimization that enables coordinated,
semantic-aware transformations.
In <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">chocolateFeast</span>, <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> identifies an algorithmic shortcut during intent refinement that reduces the time complexity of an iterative computation to <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(1)</annotation></semantics></math> and guides the subsequent optimization, achieving a <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="287.72\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>287.72</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">287.72\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup.
In <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">reverse_bits</span>, <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> achieves a <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.97\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.97</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.97\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup by coordinating multiple transformations.
After recognizing the high-level semantics of the loop as bit reversal, <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> replaces the original computation with the <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">llvm.bitreverse</span> intrinsic, and further applies an auxiliary transformation using <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">llvm.ctlz</span> with shift-based operations to model the original loop’s exit condition.
These optimizations are difficult for existing compilers to realize, as they require semantic reasoning beyond what local pattern matching in a fixed pass-by-pass pipeline can capture.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">

<span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_middle" style="width:345.0pt;">
<span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Answer to RQ.2:</span> Explicit optimization intent enables <span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> to realize optimizations that go beyond the capabilities of traditional pass-by-pass compilers.</span>
</span></span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Effectiveness of <span id="S4.SS5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> ’s Design</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The intent formulation stage is a necessary first stage in this pipeline, while intent realization serves as the final stage that generates optimized IR; neither can be bypassed.
Accordingly, our ablation study focuses on the contribution of the intent refinement stage and the impact of compiler analysis on <span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span>.
As shown in <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Improvement over Traditional Compiler ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 2</span></a>, removing intent refinement slightly improves Alive2-only correctness but leads to a noticeable degradation in both verified correctness and performance, reducing average speedup from <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.660\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.660</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.660\times</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.122\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.122</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.122\times</annotation></semantics></math>. Removing compiler analysis from both refinement and realization (<em id="S4.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">w/o Analysis</em>) further reduces verified correctness to 77.0%, as refinement and realization decisions are made without sufficient semantic constraints. Despite this, performance remains relatively high (<math id="S4.SS5.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.415\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.415</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.415\times</annotation></semantics></math> on average). This behavior can be attributed to the fact that, starting from compiler-derived optimization intents produced during intent formulation, the LLM can occasionally identify highly aggressive transformations, including the case shown in <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1.4 Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 3</span></a> that achieves a speedup of <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="287.72\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>287.72</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">287.72\times</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">

<span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_middle" style="width:345.0pt;">
<span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Answer to RQ.3:</span> Both intent refinement and compiler analysis are both critical to <span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span>, enabling effective optimization discovery and reliable realization.</span>
</span></span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper introduces <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span>, the first intent-driven IR optimization framework. By decoupling high-level optimization intent from low-level analysis and transformation, <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> addresses a critical yet underexplored dimension of IR optimization. Our experimental results show that <span id="S5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> delivers substantial improvements over both end-to-end LLM-based optimizers and traditional compiler optimizations, demonstrating that making optimization intent explicit is crucial for achieving globally coordinated, semantically sound, and high-performance IR optimization.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This work explores the use of LLMs to assist IR optimization in compilers, a domain where correctness, reliability, and performance are critical. By explicitly modeling optimization intent and separating it from low-level transformations, the proposed framework enhances the interpretability and inspectability of LLM-assisted compiler optimization, enabling developers to better understand and verify the optimization strategies produced by these systems. We believe that intent-driven optimization provides a promising foundation for future research at the intersection of compilers and machine learning, fostering more trustworthy and explainable AI-assisted program optimization.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Example of Compiler Analysis Information</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we provide a detailed example of how compiler analysis information guides the optimization process for an input IR program, as shown in <a href="#A1.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Appendix A Example of Compiler Analysis Information ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig. 6</span></a>. It contains two types of branches: (1) unconditional branch (e.g., <span id="A1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">br label %B1</span>), which is a type of branch directly jumps to another block without any conditions; (2) conditional branch (<span id="A1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">br i1 %16, label %B2, label %B3</span>), which is a type of branch performs a jump based on a condition.</p>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Dominator Tree Analysis</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Dominator Tree is a data structure used to identify the dominance relationships between basic blocks in a control flow graph (CFG) of the function. A block <span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">B</span> dominates another block <span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C</span> if every path from the entry block to <span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">C</span> must go through <span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">B</span>. The Dominator Tree helps identify potential places for optimization by highlighting which blocks are crucial for execution and which may be redundant or amenable to optimization. For the function <span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">chocolateFeast</span>, the dominator tree is shown as follows:</p>
</div>

<ul id="A1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">%B0</span> is at level 1, which indicates it is the entry block (starting point of the function). As the root of the dominator tree, <span id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">%B0</span> dominates all other blocks. It is the first block that will be executed when the function is called, and every other block must pass through it.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">%B1</span> is at level 2, meaning it is one step deeper in the control flow compared to <span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">%B0</span>. This block is dominated by <span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">%B0</span>, and it is the first block executed after <span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">%B0</span>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Both <span id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">%B2</span> and <span id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">%B3</span> are at level 3, meaning they are two steps deeper in the control flow than <span id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">%B0</span>. These blocks are dominated by <span id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">%B1</span>, meaning they are only executed after <span id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">%B1</span>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Loop Analysis</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Loops are a key target for optimization, as they are often the source of performance bottlenecks. Loop analysis identifies the loops within the function and provides details on their structure, such as their depth and the basic blocks involved. In a loop structure, the loop header is the first block in the loop, where all edges from outside the loop converge. The loop latch is a node inside the loop with an edge pointing back to the loop header. The exit block is the block where control exits the loop, marking the termination point of the loop.
For the function <span id="A1.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">chocolateFeast</span>, the loop analysis is shown as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">

<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Prompt Template for LLM-based Optimizers</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the performance of general-purpose LLM-based optimizers (GPT-5, Claude Haiku 4.5, and DeepSeek-V3.2), we use the following prompt template to guide the optimization process:</p>

<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Correctness Validation via Differential Testing</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Differential testing, also known as differential fuzzing, is a software testing technique that detects bugs by providing the same input to a series of similar applications (or to different implementations of the same application), and observing differences in their execution. Differential testing complements traditional software testing because it is well-suited to find semantic or logic bugs that do not exhibit explicit erroneous behaviors like crashes or assertion failures. In this work, we employ libFuzzer to generate a variety of inputs that cover diverse control flow paths, ensuring comprehensive testing of function behavior.</p>
</div>
<section id="A6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.1 </span>Harness Generation for Differential Testing</h3>

<div id="A6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We leverage GPT-5 to automatically generate libFuzzer harnesses for each function pair. Specifically, for each LLVM IR file containing both a base function f and its optimized variant f_opt, we prompt the LLM to synthesize a C++ fuzzing harness (fuzz.cc) using the following prompt template:</p>
</div>

<div id="A6.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The function <span id="A6.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput</span> is the entry point for libFuzzer, receiving input data generated by libFuzzer. The data is first parsed as a 32-bit integer, which is then passed as an argument to both <span id="A6.SS1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">numberOfOperations</span> and <span id="A6.SS1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">numberOfOperations_opt</span>. If the results of the base and optimized functions do not match, the program triggers a trap using <span id="A6.SS1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">__builtin_trap()</span>, halting execution and indicating a mismatch.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.2 </span>Differential Testing Binary Generation and Execution</h3>

<div id="A6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each generated harness is compiled and linked with its corresponding LLVM IR to produce an instrumented fuzzing binary. The compilation pipeline consists of:</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A6.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A6.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A6.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">IR Compilation.</span> Since <span id="A6.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">llc</span> operates on the backend, this step applies target-specific code generation and backend optimizations while preserving the IR-level transformations produced by the different optimizer.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A6.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A6.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Sanitized Linking.</span> The generated assembly is linked with the fuzzing harness (<span id="A6.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">fuzz.cc</span>) using <span id="A6.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">clang++</span>, with comprehensive sanitizer instrumentation enabled via <span id="A6.I1.i2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-fsanitize=fuzzer,address,undefined</span>. These sanitizers respectively support coverage-guided input generation, detection of memory safety violations (e.g., buffer overflows and use-after-free), and identification of undefined behavior inconsistencies between the base and optimized implementations.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Each instrumented binary is executed with 200,000 fuzzing iterations (-runs=200000). During execution, LibFuzzer continuously generates diverse test inputs guided by code coverage feedback, invoking both the base and optimized functions with identical inputs and comparing their behaviors. Any discrepancy in outputs, crashes, or sanitizer violations between the base and optimized functions indicates a semantic-altering transformation, thereby invalidating the optimization candidate. Only function pairs that successfully complete all 200,000 runs without detecting behavioral differences are validated as semantically equivalent optimizations.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Performance Validation</h2>

<div id="A7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We measure performance using the same inputs generated by libFuzzer during correctness verification, thereby reflecting execution behavior across diverse control-flow paths. Based on this design, we transform validated differential fuzzing harnesses into standalone microbenchmarks for performance measurement.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, we automatically derive microbenchmark harnesses from the validated fuzzing harnesses through a sequence of source-level transformations. Starting from a differential fuzzing harness that invokes a base function <span id="A7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">f</span> and its optimized variant <span id="A7.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">f_opt</span>, we first identify the corresponding function symbols (e.g., <span id="A7.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">numberOfOperations</span> and <span id="A7.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">numberOfOperations_opt</span> in <a href="#A6.SS1" title="F.1 Harness Generation for Differential Testing ‣ Appendix F Correctness Validation via Differential Testing ‣ Beyond Pass-by-Pass Optimization: Intent-Driven IR Optimization with Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec. F.1</span></a>). We then rename the fuzzing entry point <span id="A7.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput</span> to a standard helper function <span id="A7.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">decode_input</span>, which continues to parse raw input bytes into concrete arguments and performs a single invocation of both implementations.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Next, we inject fine-grained timing instrumentation into <span id="A7.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">decode_input</span>. As illustrated in the example, we use <span id="A7.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW)</span> to record timestamps immediately before and after each call to the base and optimized functions. Execution time and invocation counts are accumulated in global counters (e.g., <span id="A7.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">g_t_baseline_ns</span>, <span id="A7.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">g_t_opt_ns</span>). To prevent dead-code elimination, the addresses of return values are folded into a global volatile sink variable (<span id="A7.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">g_sink</span>), ensuring that both function calls are preserved by the compiler.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we synthesize a standalone <span id="A7.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">main</span> function to drive benchmarking. This driver reads concrete inputs from the fuzzing corpus, performs a fixed number of warmup iterations (e.g., 1,000 executions excluded from measurement), and then executes a large number of timed iterations (default: 1,000,000). After execution, it reports the per-call average runtime of both the base and optimized implementations, along with the resulting speedup.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p5.1" class="ltx_p">All microbenchmarks are executed on an Intel(R) Xeon(R) Gold 6434 processor, and on average, each microbenchmark is evaluated using 16.6 distinct inputs from the fuzzing corpus.</p>
</div>

<section id="A8" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix H </span>Case Study</h2>

<section id="A8.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">H.1 </span>Algorithm-level Optimization</h3>

<div id="A8.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Program Description.</span> The <span id="A8.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">chocolateFeast</span> function implements a chocolate purchasing and wrapper exchange simulation. Given an initial budget <span id="A8.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">n</span>, chocolate price <span id="A8.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">c</span>, and exchange rate <span id="A8.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">m</span> (number of wrappers needed to exchange for one chocolate), it calculates the total number of chocolates that can be consumed. The algorithm proceeds in two phases: (1) initial purchase using the budget, and (2) iterative wrapper exchanges until insufficient wrappers remain.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baseline Implementation (Unoptimized).</span> The unoptimized IR implements this logic using explicit memory allocations, repeated loads and stores, and a loop that simulates wrapper exchanges one iteration at a time.</p>
</div>

<div id="A8.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLVM <span id="A8.SS1.p4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> Optimization.</span> LLVM <span id="A8.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> performs a series of standard IR-level optimizations on the original program. First, stack-allocated scalars are promoted to SSA form via mem2reg, eliminating redundant memory operations and lifetime intrinsics. Loop-invariant computations, such as the initial division <span id="A8.SS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">q=n/c</span>, are hoisted out of the loop, and loop-carried values are represented using PHI nodes. As a result, the optimized IR produced by LLVM <span id="A8.SS1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> expresses the wrapper-exchange process more compactly in SSA form and removes unnecessary memory traffic. However, the core computation remains a loop that repeatedly updates the number of wrappers and consumed chocolates.</p>

<div id="A8.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt<span id="A8.SS1.p6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">.</span></span> In contrast, <span id="A8.SS1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> goes beyond structural IR cleanup and performs algorithm-level reasoning. After applying the same foundational optimizations as LLVM <span id="A8.SS1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> – such as SSA promotion, loop canonicalization, and invariant hoisting – <span id="A8.SS1.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> identifies a key mathematical property of the wrapper-exchange process.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, when <span id="A8.SS1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">m</span> <math id="A8.SS1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math> and <span id="A8.SS1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">q</span> <math id="A8.SS1.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, the number of additional chocolates obtained through wrapper exchanges can be computed in closed form as:</p>
<table id="A8.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A8.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\lfloor\frac{q-1}{m-1}\right\rfloor" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>⌊</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>⌋</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\lfloor\frac{q-1}{m-1}\right\rfloor</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A8.SS1.p7.2" class="ltx_p">Based on this observation, <span id="A8.SS1.p7.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> introduces a fast path that directly computes the total number of chocolates as:</p>
<table id="A8.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A8.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q+\left\lfloor\frac{q-1}{m-1}\right\rfloor" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo>⌊</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>⌋</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q+\left\lfloor\frac{q-1}{m-1}\right\rfloor</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A8.SS1.p7.3" class="ltx_p">completely eliminating the loop in this common case. Importantly, boundary checks are preserved: the fast path is only taken when <span id="A8.SS1.p7.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">m</span> <math id="A8.SS1.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math>, avoiding division-by-zero and ensuring semantic equivalence with the original program. For remaining cases, <span id="A8.SS1.p7.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> falls back to a canonicalized loop that mirrors the original behavior, including non-termination when <span id="A8.SS1.p7.3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">m</span> <math id="A8.SS1.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq 1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>

<div id="lstnumberx312" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx312.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">-</span><span id="lstnumberx312.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx312.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#00B300;">Add a fast closed-form path for m &gt; 1</span>

<div id="lstnumberx313" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx313.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">  </span><span id="lstnumberx313.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">-</span><span id="lstnumberx313.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx313.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#00B300;">When m &gt; 1 and the initial quotient q &gt; 0, the number of exchanges is floor((q - 1) / (m - 1)). Return q + floor((q - 1) / (m - 1)) without entering the loop.</span>

<div id="lstnumberx314" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx314.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">  </span><span id="lstnumberx314.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">-</span><span id="lstnumberx314.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx314.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#00B300;">Keep boundary checks: do not compute (q - 1) / (m - 1) unless m &gt; 1 to avoid division by zero. For other cases, fall back to the loop, preserving original behavior (including non-termination for m &lt;= 1).</span>

</div>
<div id="A8.SS1.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS1.p12.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.p12.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Discussion.</span> This example highlights a fundamental distinction between traditional compiler optimizations and intent-driven optimization. LLVM <span id="A8.SS1.p12.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> improves performance by restructuring the program within the same algorithmic framework, whereas <span id="A8.SS1.p12.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> recognizes and exploits a higher-level mathematical invariant of the algorithm itself. By replacing an iterative process with a closed-form computation under well-defined conditions, <span id="A8.SS1.p12.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> achieves an optimization that is fundamentally algorithmic rather than purely syntactic or structural.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A8.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">H.2 </span>Global-coordinated Optimization</h3>

<section id="A8.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">H.2.1 </span>reverse_bit</h4>

<div id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Program Description.</span> This function implements a data-dependent bit-reversal routine. Starting from an input integer <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">n</span>, it iteratively constructs an output accumulator by (1) shifting the accumulator left by one bit, (2) appending the current least-significant bit of <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">n</span>, and (3) shifting <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">n</span> right by one bit. The loop terminates when <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">n=0</span>. Intuitively, the function returns the bit-reversal of the significant prefix of <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">n</span>: it reverses the bits of <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">n</span> up to its most-significant 1-bit, while ignoring leading zeros. For example, <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">n</span>=6 (<span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">110b</span>) yields <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">011b</span> (=3).</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baseline Implementation (Unoptimized).</span> The unoptimized IR expresses the algorithm in a literal, step-by-step manner. It allocates stack slots for the input, the accumulator, and a temporary bit, and repeatedly performs memory loads/stores inside the loop.</p>

<div id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLVM <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> Optimization.</span> LLVM <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> performs canonical IR cleanups and loop simplification. It promotes stack-allocated variables to SSA (mem2reg), removes lifetime intrinsics, and represents the loop-carried state using PHI nodes: one PHI for the evolving input value and one for the accumulator.</p>

<div id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt<span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">.</span></span> <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> identifies the loop as an instance of bit reversal and realizes it using a coordinated transformation that spans multiple abstraction levels: (1) semantic recognition of the loop’s algorithmic intent, (2) selection of hardware-mappable LLVM intrinsics, and (3) careful boundary handling to preserve defined behavior. Concretely, <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> replaces the entire loop with two compiler intrinsics: <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">llvm.bitreverse.i32</span> to reverse all 32 bits of <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">n</span>, and <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">llvm.ctlz.i32</span> (with <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p4.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">is_zero_undef=false</span>) to compute the number of leading zeros.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The refined strategy generated by <span id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> is as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<div id="A8.SS2.SSS1.p6.1" class="ltx_listing ltx_lstlisting ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle ltx_listing" style="--ltx-border-color:#FFFFFF;"><div class="ltx_listing_data"><a href="data:text/plain;base64," download="">⬇</a></div>
<div id="lstnumberx405" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx405.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">-</span><span id="lstnumberx405.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx405.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#00B300;">Replace the loop with two data-dependent instructions that the backend can map to hardware:</span><span id="lstnumberx405.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx405.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#00B300;">llvm.bitreverse.i32 to reverse all 32 bits, and llvm.ctlz.i32 (with is_zero_undef=false) to compute the number of leading zeros. The final result is lshr(bitreverse(n), ctlz(n)), which exactly matches the original loop’s semantics for non-negative inputs and avoids undefined behavior by guarding n==0.</span>
</div>

<section id="A8.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">H.2.2 </span>_Z3conii</h4>

<div id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Program Description.</span> The function returns a Boolean-like integer (<math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>) based on a set of guarded conditions. Intuitively, it checks whether the integer <math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> equals the number of decimal digits of <math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>, under additional validity constraints: <math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\in[1,m)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\in[1,m)</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> is a global threshold, and a special boundary case when <math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=0</annotation></semantics></math>. The unoptimized implementation computes the digit count as <math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lfloor\log_{10}(y)\rfloor+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌊</mo><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mn>10</mn></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌋</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lfloor\log_{10}(y)\rfloor+1</annotation></semantics></math> and compares it with <math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, returning <math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> iff they match; otherwise it returns <math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baseline Implementation (Unoptimized).</span> The unoptimized IR implements the logic using multiple basic blocks and stack-based temporaries. It computes <math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lfloor\log_{10}(y)\rfloor+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌊</mo><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mn>10</mn></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌋</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lfloor\log_{10}(y)\rfloor+1</annotation></semantics></math> via integer-to-floating-point conversion, a math-library call to <span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">log10</span>, and a floating-point-to-integer cast.</p>
</div>

<div id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLVM <span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> Optimization.</span>
LLVM <span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">-O3</span> applies standard IR-level optimizations, including promoting stack variables to SSA form, collapsing redundant basic blocks, and simplifying control flow using PHI nodes and <span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">select</span> instructions. These transformations reduce memory traffic and streamline the control flow. However, the optimized IR still relies on the floating-point digit-count computation using <span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">log10</span>.</p>
</div>

<div id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt<span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">.</span></span>
<span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> performs a global-coordinated optimization by combining data-flow analysis with semantic reasoning over library calls. By tracing the provenance of the argument passed to <span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">log10</span>, <span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> recognizes that the computation operates on the integer input <math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> and that its numeric domain is tightly constrained by preceding control-flow guards. This enables <span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p6.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> to reinterpret the floating-point expression <math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lfloor\log_{10}(y)\rfloor+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌊</mo><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mn>10</mn></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌋</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lfloor\log_{10}(y)\rfloor+1</annotation></semantics></math> as an integer digit-count operation rather than a general library call.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Based on this reinterpretation, <span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> replaces the floating-point conversion and library call with a semantically equivalent integer formulation. The digit count is computed exactly using a sequence of comparisons against constant powers of ten (e.g., <math id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\geq 10,100,1000,\ldots" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>10,100</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1000</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\geq 10,100,1000,\ldots</annotation></semantics></math>), followed by accumulation of the Boolean results.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">The refined strategy generated by <span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> is as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS2.SSS2.p9" class="ltx_para">

<div id="lstnumberx508" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx508.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">-</span><span id="lstnumberx508.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx508.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#00B300;">Strength-reduce and eliminate the floating-point path:</span><span id="lstnumberx508.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx508.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#00B300;">Replace the floor(log10(%1)) + 1 digit-count using the math library with an exact, branchless integer computation of decimal digits based on comparisons against constant powers of 10. <section id="A8.SS2.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Discussion.</h5>

<div id="A8.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This example highlights the advantage of <span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> ’s global-coordinated optimization guided by optimization intent. <span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> recognizing the semantic role of the computation, validating its applicability via global guards, and selecting an implementation that better aligns with the target execution model. As a result, <span id="A8.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IntOpt</span> performs an optimization that spans multiple abstraction layers, demonstrating how global coordination enables performance improvements beyond the reach of conventional compiler pipelines.</p>
</div>
</section>
